questions.q: What four parts make up the lesson's framework for answering an AI system design question?
options: Budget, team size, timeline, and marketing plan
Requirements, architecture, tradeoffs, and failure modes
Programming language, framework, IDE, and operating system
Company name, job title, salary, and start date
questions.explain: The lesson's framework moves through requirements, architecture, tradeoffs, and failure modes for almost any AI system design prompt.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say pinning down requirements should come before sketching architecture?
options: Because architecture diagrams are not allowed in interviews
Because requirements have no real effect on which architecture makes sense
Because scale, latency tolerance, and the cost of being wrong should shape the architecture, not be fit to it afterward
Because interviewers only ever care about the programming language used
questions.explain: The lesson frames requirements -- scale, latency, and the cost of being wrong -- as the input that should shape the architecture decisions that follow.

questions.q: In the worked RAG-for-policy-questions example, what does the lesson say the system should do when retrieval confidence is low?
options: Shut down entirely and refuse to answer any future questions
Generate the most confident-sounding answer possible regardless of retrieval quality
Say it couldn't find a confident answer and log the query, rather than guessing
Ignore the retrieved documents and answer from general knowledge instead
questions.explain: The worked example's failure-mode step calls for an honest 'I couldn't find a confident answer' response and logging the query for follow-up, instead of a forced guess.

questions.q: In the worked refund-agent example, why does the lesson say the refund tool needs to be idempotent?
options: So that a retry after a timeout can't accidentally issue a duplicate refund
So that the agent never needs a human approval checkpoint
So that refunds can be issued without checking order history
So that the system can skip logging each step
questions.explain: The lesson names idempotency specifically to prevent a retried call after a timeout from double-refunding the same request.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the 'failure modes' step is the one that most signals production experience?
options: Because it is the easiest step and takes the least time to explain
Because it is required by every company's style guide
Because it is the step most candidates skip, and naming a failure plus its safeguard shows real operational thinking
Because it replaces the need to discuss architecture at all
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls failure modes the step most candidates skip, and says naming a failure together with its safeguard is what signals production-level thinking.
